h1: Czech SEO for Two Search Engines, Not One
intro:
Czechia is the EU market where Google-only SEO visibly fails. Google holds 82 to 85 percent of Czech searches as of 2025, which sounds dominant until you meet the other player: Seznam.cz, the homegrown Czech search engine, with 11 to 15 percent. That is the highest local search engine share anywhere in the EU, and it represents roughly every ninth Czech searcher. Ignore Seznam and you hand one-ninth of the market to competitors. I optimize for both engines, because in Czechia both engines have customers.

Seznam is not just a search box. It is an ecosystem Czechs use daily: Mapy.cz for maps and navigation, Firmy.cz as the business directory, Zprávy for news, and Zboží.cz for shopping. A Czech looking for a local service may never touch Google. They search Seznam, check the firm on Firmy.cz, and navigate with Mapy.cz. If your business is absent from that loop, you are absent from a meaningful slice of Czech commercial intent. Google knows this too: AI Overviews arrived in Czechia in May 2025, and AI Mode rolled out from October 7, 2025, so the zero-click shift is live on both fronts.

The business geography centers on Prague, the capital and economic engine, with Brno as the tech and university hub and Ostrava anchoring industry. Manufacturing runs deep: automotive, led by Škoda, is a pillar, and the supplier ecosystem generates serious B2B search demand. The koruna remains the currency, Czechia has not adopted the euro, so commercial content prices in CZK and gets the schema markup to match. Czech business culture is formal and Czech-language loyal. Customers search in Czech, read reviews in Czech, and trust businesses that communicate in proper Czech.

Seznam's confidence tells its own story: in 2026 it sued Google for about 417 million dollars over Android competition restrictions, a sign of a local champion that intends to keep its share. My Czechia playbook treats the dual-engine reality as the core strategic fact. Czech-language keyword research done properly, Firmy.cz and Mapy.cz listings claimed and optimized, Google Business Profile excellence for the Google majority, review strategies in Czech, and content with the depth to earn both rankings and AI citations. One engine is a gamble. Two engines is a strategy.  The numbers frame the opportunity precisely. Google holds 82 to 85 percent of Czech searches as of 2025, and Seznam.cz holds 11 to 15 percent, the highest local engine share anywhere in the EU. Roughly every ninth Czech searcher uses Seznam, and they cluster exactly where local commercial intent lives. Seznam's own confidence shows in its actions: in 2026 it sued Google for about 417 million dollars over Android competition restrictions, a local champion fighting to keep its share. My Czechia playbook treats the dual-engine reality as the core strategic fact: Czech-language keyword research done properly, Firmy.cz and Mapy.cz listings claimed and optimized, Google Business Profile excellence for the Google majority, and content deep enough to earn both rankings and AI citations.

why.heading: Why Czechia Demands a Dual-Engine SEO Strategy
why.body:
The Seznam factor is the whole story. In every other EU market I work in, Google's share rounds to effectively all of search, and optimizing for Google is optimizing for the market. Czechia breaks that rule. Seznam's 11 to 15 percent is concentrated exactly where local commercial intent lives: Czech-language queries, local services, maps. Seznam's users skew toward Czechs who prefer domestic platforms, which correlates with the customers most likely to buy from a local business. A Google-only strategy does not just miss traffic. It misses the most locally-rooted buyers.

The two engines also behave differently. Seznam's algorithm weighs Czech-language relevance, local signals, and its own ecosystem data from Firmy.cz and Mapy.cz. Tactics that work on Google transfer partially but not fully. Firmy.cz listings, for example, function as both citations and a discovery channel: Czechs browse the directory directly. Mapy.cz business profiles put you on the map Czechs actually navigate with. I build and optimize these as first-class assets, not afterthoughts.

Czech language quality is a competitive moat. Czechs notice bad Czech instantly, and machine-translated content ranks poorly and converts worse. Proper Czech keyword research matters enormously because Czech morphology, with its cases and diacritics, creates query variants that lazy research misses entirely. I work in real Czech, with diacritics handled correctly and declensions accounted for in the keyword mapping.

Finally, Prague's B2B market adds an English layer. International companies and tech firms in Prague search partly in English, so many Czech B2B sites need Czech foundations plus English pages for the international segment. Specialized Czechia SEO means holding all of this at once: both engines, proper Czech, Prague's bilingual B2B reality, and koruna-correct commercial content. It is more work than single-engine SEO. It is also why it wins.  Czech morphology is a quiet technical challenge that most foreign agencies never notice. Czech is a heavily inflected language: nouns change form across seven cases, and diacritics distinguish meanings. Lazy keyword research in Czech misses entire families of query variants, and lazy content reads as foreign, which Czechs spot instantly. I build keyword maps that account for declensions and handle diacritics correctly throughout. This sounds like a detail. In Czech SEO it is a competitive advantage, because so many competitors, especially international ones, get it wrong. Proper Czech is a moat.

section1.heading: Citations and Directories Across Both Czech Engines
section1.body:
Czech citations live in two ecosystems, and most foreign agencies only know one. On the Seznam side, Firmy.cz is the essential business directory: it is Seznam's own, Czechs browse it directly, and it feeds Seznam's local relevance signals. Claiming and completing your Firmy.cz listing, with correct Czech categories, photos, and details, is the single highest-value citation action in Czechia. Next to it, a Mapy.cz business profile puts you on the maps Czechs navigate with daily. These two are non-negotiable.

Najisto.cz is another established Czech business catalog worth a correct listing. Kompass covers the B2B and industrial side. On the Google side, the standard work applies: your Google Business Profile as the anchor citation, international aggregators audited for consistency, duplicates removed, old data fixed. I run the full audit across both ecosystems because an error on Firmy.cz costs you Seznam visibility while an error on Google costs you the majority.

Czech-language consistency is the thread through all of it. Your business name, address formats, and category descriptions need to match in proper Czech with diacritics correct. Mixed or transliterated variants split your entity signals across the two engines. I standardize everything, claim what is unclaimed, fix what is wrong, and build the profiles Czech customers actually encounter. Dual-engine citations are twice the detail work, and detail work is the job.  Zboží.cz deserves a mention for Czech e-commerce: Seznam's shopping engine feeds product visibility for Czech shoppers who never touch Google Shopping. If you sell products, Zboží feeds and optimization are part of the Seznam-side strategy. For services, the equivalent discovery channel is Firmy.cz browsing, where Czechs look up trades and services directly. Najisto.cz adds another established catalog. The principle is the same on both engines: be present where the Czech customer is already looking, with complete, accurate, Czech-language information. I map every relevant surface per client rather than applying a one-size citation package, because Czechia's dual ecosystem makes generic packages particularly wasteful.

section2.heading: Owning Local Search on Google and Mapy.cz
section2.body:
In Czechia you win local search twice or you lose half of it. On Google, the map pack works as everywhere: complete profile, correct Czech categories, real photos, review velocity with substance, posts, and Q&A. Prague's pack is competitive, Brno's less so, and both reward the profile that looks most alive and most local. I build Google profiles to that standard, with review processes that generate steady Czech-language reviews and owner replies in proper Czech.

On Seznam's side, Mapy.cz is where the second victory happens. Czechs who navigate with Mapy.cz discover businesses through it directly, and a complete Mapy.cz business profile with photos, hours, and correct categorization captures demand Google never sees. Firmy.cz reviews add another layer: Czechs check them, and they feed Seznam's trust signals. I treat these as parallel profile systems, each maintained to the same standard.

Review culture in Czechia rewards substance. Czech customers write detailed reviews when motivated and read them skeptically, so I focus on earning specific, credible Czech reviews rather than gaming volume. Responses in correct Czech, addressing the substance of the review, convert readers. Between Google's majority and Seznam's loyal minority, the businesses that maintain both presences completely pull away from competitors who only bothered with one. That gap is where I put my clients.  Brno deserves its own note as the second market. It is the tech and university hub, with a younger, digital-native audience and competitive local packs in services. Ostrava's industrial economy generates B2B search demand around manufacturing and engineering services. Each city gets its own profile and content strategy rather than a Prague template with the name swapped. Review dynamics differ too: Brno's younger customers review more readily, Ostrava's B2B buyers research longer. I calibrate the review and content approach per city. Dual engines, multiple cities, proper Czech: this is more work than single-engine SEO, and it is exactly why it wins. One more Czech-specific point: Seznam lets users plan trips with saved places inside Mapy.cz, which means a well-maintained Mapy.cz profile keeps working for you inside travel planning, not just local search. I optimize for that discovery path too. Between Google and Seznam, the businesses that maintain both presences pull away from competitors who only bothered with one engine, and that gap widens every month.

faqs.q: Is optimizing for Seznam really necessary, or is Google enough?
faqs.a: It is necessary. Seznam's 11 to 15 percent is roughly every ninth Czech searcher, concentrated in Czech-language local queries, exactly the commercial intent local businesses want. Google-only SEO hands that ninth to competitors. I optimize for both engines because in Czechia, both engines have paying customers.

faqs.q: What is Firmy.cz and how do I claim my listing?
faqs.a: Firmy.cz is Seznam's business directory, browsed directly by Czechs and feeding Seznam's local signals. Claiming means verifying your business, completing every field in proper Czech, adding photos, and keeping details current. I handle the claim, the optimization, and the ongoing maintenance as part of the citation work.

faqs.q: Should I also maintain a Mapy.cz listing?
faqs.a: Yes. Mapy.cz is the map many Czechs navigate with daily, and its business profiles are a discovery channel Google never sees. A complete Mapy.cz profile with photos, hours, and correct categories captures Seznam-loyal demand. I build and maintain it alongside your Google Business Profile as a parallel system.

faqs.q: Czech or English content for a Prague B2B company?
faqs.a: Czech foundations first, English where the buyers are international. Prague's tech and corporate scene searches partly in English, so B2B companies often need both: Czech pages for domestic buyers, English pages for the international segment, with hreflang keeping them straight. I map this per business during the audit.

faqs.q: My shop prices in koruna. Any SEO implications?
faqs.a: Yes, practical ones. Prices should display in CZK, schema markup should declare priceCurrency as CZK, and content should never show euro-only pricing that confuses Czech buyers. I audit commercial pages for currency correctness as part of technical SEO, because mismatched pricing kills conversion at the finish line.
